enfeeble

en-FEE-buhl · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To enfeeble is to make someone or something weak.

The prolonged drought began to enfeeble even the hardiest crops in the region.

Example

Years of neglect had enfeebled the old bridge so badly that engineers finally closed it to traffic.

Enfeeble describes the process of making something weak over time, whether it's a person's health, a structure, or even an argument that's been picked apart.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

weaken: Weaken is the plain, everyday word for making something less strong, and it fits any register and any subject. Enfeeble means the same basic act but is formal and old-fashioned, and it usually pictures strength being drained gradually, bit by bit, over a long stretch of time.

debilitate: To debilitate is to weaken someone or something so severely that normal life or normal working nearly stops — a debilitating illness keeps a person in bed for weeks. Enfeeble is slower and less total: it drains strength gradually while everyday life limps on.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

strengthen: make stronger

fortify: give added strength to

Where it sits · how lasting the weakening is — tire → enfeeble → cripple

tire vs. enfeeble: To tire someone is far milder than to enfeeble them: tiredness lifts after a night's rest, while an enfeebled body has lost strength that rest alone will not bring back.

cripple vs. enfeeble: To cripple something is to damage it so severely it may never fully recover, a step beyond simply enfeebling it.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — en-

prefix — en-: to make, to cause to be (Old French)

root — feeble

root — feeble: weak (Old French (feble, from Latin flebilis, "lamentable"))

Put it together

Put it together: en- ("to make") + feeble ("weak") = to make weak.

Use the root in a new word: feebleness

Use the root in a new word: feebleness: The same root gives us "feebleness," the plain noun for the state of being weak.

Word Building

Word Choice

Enfeeble is a fairly formal, almost old-fashioned word -- in everyday conversation, 'weaken' does the same job with a far more casual, modern feel. Its own root, "feeble," is itself a word you already met earlier in this course.
